import pytest
from target import age_in_years


def test_exact_birthday_match():
    # Equality boundary: (on_month, on_day) == (birth_month, birth_day) -> lt is False, no decrement
    assert age_in_years(2000, 5, 15, 2026, 5, 15) == 26


def test_day_before_birthday():
    # Day boundary: on_day = birth_day - 1, same month -> lt True, age decremented
    assert age_in_years(2000, 5, 15, 2026, 5, 14) == 25


def test_day_after_birthday():
    # Day boundary: on_day = birth_day + 1, same month -> lt False, no decrement
    assert age_in_years(2000, 5, 15, 2026, 5, 16) == 26


def test_month_only_boundary():
    # Month boundary: on_month < birth_month decides the branch regardless of day
    assert age_in_years(2000, 3, 10, 2026, 2, 28) == 25


def test_counterexample_naive_month_only_check():
    # SMT-derived counterexample: Z3 refuted lt == (on_month < birth_month).
    # Here om==bm, od<bd -> lt=True, but a naive "month-only" comparator would say False
    # and wrongly return 36 instead of the correct 35.
    assert age_in_years(1990, 6, 20, 2026, 6, 5) == 35


def test_counterexample_naive_day_only_check():
    # SMT-derived counterexample: om>bm, od<bd under a valid precondition.
    # Correct lexicographic compare -> lt=False (month dominates), age=36.
    # A naive "day-only" comparator would wrongly return 35.
    assert age_in_years(1990, 3, 20, 2026, 4, 5) == 36


def test_leap_day_birthday_day_before_in_nonleap_year():
    # Boundary: birth on Feb 29 (leap year 2000), evaluated one day before the
    # anniversary (Feb 28) in a non-leap year (2026) -> lt True, decrement applies
    assert age_in_years(2000, 2, 29, 2026, 2, 28) == 25


def test_leap_day_birthday_day_after_in_nonleap_year():
    # Boundary: same leap-day birthday, evaluated the day after (Mar 1) in a
    # non-leap year -> on_month(3) > birth_month(2), lt False, no decrement
    assert age_in_years(2000, 2, 29, 2026, 3, 1) == 26


def test_december_to_january_month_wraparound():
    # Month/year wraparound boundary: Dec 31 birth vs Jan 1 "on" date -> lt True
    assert age_in_years(1999, 12, 31, 2026, 1, 1) == 26


def test_day_one_boundary_exact_match():
    # Day boundary edge value: birth_day == on_day == 1, same month, exact match
    assert age_in_years(2000, 7, 1, 2026, 7, 1) == 26


def test_same_year_birth_and_on_date_age_zero():
    # Equivalence class: birth date == on date in the same year -> age 0
    assert age_in_years(2026, 7, 8, 2026, 7, 8) == 0


def test_on_date_equals_birth_date_general():
    # Equivalence class: general representative of "on-date == birth-date" -> age 0
    assert age_in_years(2015, 9, 23, 2015, 9, 23) == 0


def test_many_years_elapsed_birthday_already_passed():
    # Equivalence class: many years elapsed, birthday already occurred this year
    # (on_month > birth_month) -> no decrement
    assert age_in_years(1950, 1, 10, 2026, 6, 15) == 76


def test_many_years_elapsed_birthday_not_yet_reached():
    # Equivalence class: many years elapsed, birthday not yet reached this year
    # (on_month < birth_month) -> decrement applies
    assert age_in_years(1950, 12, 25, 2026, 6, 15) == 75

import pytest
from target import binary_search


# ---- n = 0 boundary: while lo<=hi guard, lo=0,hi=-1 -> loop never executes ----
def test_empty_array():
    # Boundary: n=0 => lo=0, hi=len-1=-1, violates lo<=hi immediately (first violation of loop guard).
    assert binary_search([], 3) == -1


# ---- n = 1 boundary: match and no-match ----
def test_single_element_match():
    # Boundary: n=1, mid=(0+0)//2=0, items[0]==target -> equality point of mid formula.
    assert binary_search([7], 7) == 0


def test_single_element_no_match():
    # Boundary: n=1, items[0]!=target (both < and > branches collapse to same no-match outcome).
    assert binary_search([7], 3) == -1


# ---- n = 2 boundary: mid=(0+1)//2=0 always; exercise both possible resolutions ----
def test_two_elements_match_at_mid0():
    # Boundary: n=2 => mid0=0 (proved via Z3: (0+1)//2==0). items[0]==target -> immediate match branch.
    assert binary_search([3, 9], 3) == 0


def test_two_elements_match_at_index1():
    # Boundary: n=2, mid0=0 misses (items[0]<target) -> lo=1, mid1=1, items[1]==target.
    # Trace verified via smt_verify: mid0=0, mid1=1, result=1, loop terminates.
    assert binary_search([3, 9], 9) == 1


def test_two_elements_gap_not_present():
    # Equivalence class: gap_absent, minimal n=2 case.
    # mid0=0 (3<5) -> lo=1; mid1=1 (9>5) -> hi=0; loop ends, not found.
    assert binary_search([3, 9], 5) == -1


# ---- Equivalence classes derived via csp_solve over {n, target_class} ----

def test_below_all():
    # Equivalence class: target smaller than every element (would insert at index 0).
    # Trace verified: mid0=2(6)>1->hi=1; mid1=0(2)>1->hi=-1; loop ends. final=-1.
    assert binary_search([2, 4, 6, 8, 10], 1) == -1


def test_above_all():
    # Equivalence class: target larger than every element (would insert at end).
    # Trace verified: mid0=2(6)<99->lo=3; mid1=3(8)<99->lo=4; mid2=4(10)<99->lo=5; loop ends. final=-1.
    assert binary_search([2, 4, 6, 8, 10], 99) == -1


def test_match_first():
    # Boundary: target at index 0 of a larger array (n=5).
    # Trace verified: mid0=2(6)>2->hi=1; mid1=0(2)==2->result=0,hi=-1; loop ends. final=0.
    assert binary_search([2, 4, 6, 8, 10], 2) == 0


def test_match_last():
    # Boundary: target at index n-1 (n=5).
    # Trace verified: mid0=2(6)<10->lo=3; mid1=3(8)<10->lo=4; mid2=4(10)==10->result=4,hi=3; loop ends. final=4.
    assert binary_search([2, 4, 6, 8, 10], 10) == 4


def test_match_unique_mid():
    # Equivalence class: target present exactly once, at the array's structural midpoint.
    # Trace verified: mid0=2(6)==6->result=2,hi=1; mid1=0(2)<6->lo=1; mid2=1(4)<6->lo=2; loop ends. final=2.
    assert binary_search([2, 4, 6, 8, 10], 6) == 2


def test_gap_between_elements():
    # Equivalence class: target absent, falls in a gap between two existing elements (4 and 6).
    # Trace verified: mid0=2(6)>5->hi=1; mid1=0(2)<5->lo=1; mid2=1(4)<5->lo=2; loop ends. final=-1.
    assert binary_search([2, 4, 6, 8, 10], 5) == -1


def test_duplicate_run_in_middle():
    # Equivalence class: target present multiple times as a contiguous run in the middle (n=7).
    # Trace verified: mid0=3(5)==5->result=3,hi=2; mid1=1(2)<5->lo=2; mid2=2(5)==5->result=2,hi=1; loop ends.
    # Confirms the leftward hi=mid-1 bias walks the result back to the FIRST duplicate (index 2), not 3.
    assert binary_search([1, 2, 5, 5, 5, 5, 9], 5) == 2


def test_duplicate_run_at_start():
    # Equivalence class: target present multiple times, run starts at index 0 (n=5).
    # Trace verified: mid0=2(3)==3->result=2,hi=1; mid1=0(3)==3->result=0,hi=-1; loop ends. final=0.
    assert binary_search([3, 3, 3, 7, 9], 3) == 0


# ---- Counterexample class: FIRST occurrence vs "any occurrence" ----

def test_all_duplicates_returns_first_index_not_middle():
    # Counterexample class (n=7, every element == target).
    # Solver-proved trace: mid0=3 (r=3,hi=2), mid1=1 (r=1,hi=0), mid2=0 (r=0,hi=-1), loop terminates with result=0.
    # A naive "stop at first match" implementation would wrongly return 3 (the initial mid).
    # The docstring mandates the FIRST occurrence, so 0 is the only correct answer.
    assert binary_search([4, 4, 4, 4, 4, 4, 4], 4) == 0


def test_large_duplicate_run_not_at_boundary_first_occurrence():
    # Counterexample class (n=9): 6 duplicates of target=3 occupy indices 2..7, flanked by 1,2 and 9.
    # Solver-proved: a naive/any-match variant's first hit is mid0=4 (result=4) -- INDEX 4 IS WRONG.
    # Real algorithm continues left via hi=mid-1: mid1=1(2<3)->lo=2; mid2=2(3==3)->result=2; loop ends
    # (lo=2 > hi=1). Proved final result == 2, matching the true first occurrence.
    # This is the decisive test that fails for any "returns *a* matching index" implementation
    # that lacks the leftward hi=mid-1 bias on equality.
    assert binary_search([1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 9], 3) == 2

import pytest
from target import ceil_div


# --- Docstring / sanity examples (also exact-division and remainder-1 witnesses) ---

def test_docstring_example_remainder_nonzero():
    # ceil_div(7,2): remainder-of-(d-1) style non-exact case, docstring example.
    # Z3: numerator = k*d+1 class (k=3,d=2) proved q==k+1==4 -> inconsistent (proved).
    assert ceil_div(7, 2) == 4


def test_docstring_example_exact_division_not_rounded_up():
    # ceil_div(8,2): exact division (numerator = k*denominator, k=4).
    # Z3 general-exact-division check (k>=1) proved q==k -> inconsistent (proved).
    # Also matches the naive-formula divergence class (naive would give 5).
    assert ceil_div(8, 2) == 4


def test_docstring_example_numerator_zero():
    # ceil_div(0,5): numerator=0 boundary class, symbolic proof for all denominator>=1
    # (denominator=1..inf) came back inconsistent (proved q==0).
    assert ceil_div(0, 5) == 0


# --- numerator = 0 boundary (denominator=1 edge of that class) ---

def test_numerator_zero_denominator_one():
    # Boundary intersection of "numerator==0" class and "denominator==1" class.
    # Z3 proof of numerator=0 class (any denominator>=1) -> inconsistent (proved q==0).
    assert ceil_div(0, 1) == 0


# --- denominator = 1 identity class ---

def test_denominator_one_identity_nonzero():
    # denominator=1 identity class: Z3 proved q == numerator for all numerator>=0
    # (inconsistent verdict = proved).
    assert ceil_div(7, 1) == 7


def test_denominator_one_identity_large():
    # Same identity class, larger representative to sanity check no truncation.
    assert ceil_div(100, 1) == 100


# --- Exact division class: numerator = k*denominator, k>=1 ---

def test_exact_division_k1():
    # k=1 boundary of exact-division class (numerator==denominator exactly).
    # Z3 proved q==k for all k>=1, denominator>=1 -> inconsistent (proved).
    assert ceil_div(5, 5) == 1


def test_exact_division_k2():
    # k=2 representative of exact-division equivalence class.
    assert ceil_div(6, 3) == 2


def test_exact_division_naive_formula_counterexample():
    # Counterexample from Z3 that distinguishes correct formula from the
    # naive "numerator // denominator + 1" formula: model found
    # numerator=3, denominator=3 -> correct=1, naive=2 (consistent verdict,
    # i.e. a real divergence exists). This is precisely the "exact division
    # must NOT be rounded up" rule from the docstring.
    assert ceil_div(3, 3) == 1


def test_exact_division_large():
    # Large exact-division instance (2**31 / 2**16 = 2**15 exactly).
    # Covered in principle by the unbounded-integer proof above; included
    # concretely since Python ints are the implementation's actual domain.
    assert ceil_div(2**31, 2**16) == 32768


# --- Remainder-of-1 class: numerator = k*denominator + 1, k>=0, denominator>=2 ---

def test_remainder_one_k0():
    # k=0 boundary of remainder-1 class == also the "numerator < denominator" class
    # (numerator=1 < denominator=5). Z3 proved q==k+1==1 -> inconsistent (proved).
    assert ceil_div(1, 5) == 1


def test_remainder_one_k2():
    # k=2 interior representative of the remainder-1 class.
    assert ceil_div(7, 3) == 3


# --- Worst-case remainder class: numerator = k*denominator + (denominator-1) ---

def test_worst_case_remainder_k0():
    # k=0 boundary: numerator = denominator-1 (largest possible remainder, still < denominator).
    # Z3 proved q==k+1==1 -> inconsistent (proved).
    assert ceil_div(4, 5) == 1


def test_worst_case_remainder_k2():
    # k=2 interior representative of worst-case-remainder class.
    # Z3 proved q==k+1==3 -> inconsistent (proved).
    assert ceil_div(14, 5) == 3


# --- numerator < denominator class boundary transition (n=d-1, n=d, n=d+1) ---

def test_boundary_below_equal_and_above_denominator():
    # Exhaustive boundary triple around numerator == denominator (d=5):
    # n=4 (numerator<denominator, worst-case-remainder k=0) -> 1
    # n=5 (exact division, k=1)                              -> 1
    # n=6 (remainder-1, k=1)                                  -> 2
    # First two classes proved "inconsistent" (proved) individually above;
    # this test pins the exact transition point where the result increments.
    assert ceil_div(4, 5) == 1
    assert ceil_div(5, 5) == 1
    assert ceil_div(6, 5) == 2


# --- Large numerator/denominator, non-exact ---

def test_large_values_nonexact():
    # Large representative outside all small hand-picked classes above;
    # covered by the general symbolic proof (unbounded ints, no overflow
    # since Python ints are arbitrary precision).
    assert ceil_div(1_000_000_007, 1_000) == 1_000_001

import pytest
from target import count_multiples_in_range


# --- 1. start == end, start is an exact multiple of divisor ---
# Boundary: start == end (single-element range).
# CSP: SAT@1 with k=12 (12%4==0), UNSAT@2 -> true count is exactly 1.
# SMT: proved end/divisor - (start-1)/divisor == 1 for (12,12,4).
def test_start_equals_end_exact_multiple():
    assert count_multiples_in_range(12, 12, 4) == 1


# --- 2. start == end, start is NOT a multiple of divisor ---
# Boundary: start == end. CSP: UNSAT@1 (13 % 4 != 0) -> count is 0.
def test_start_equals_end_not_multiple():
    assert count_multiples_in_range(13, 13, 4) == 0


# --- 3. divisor == 1 (documented lower bound on divisor) ---
# Equality point of constraint divisor >= 1.
# SMT: proved end/divisor - (start-1)/divisor == end - start + 1 for divisor==1.
def test_divisor_one_counts_every_integer():
    assert count_multiples_in_range(7, 19, 1) == 13


# --- 4. start == 1 (documented lower bound on start; start-1 == 0) ---
# CSP: SAT@3 with {3,6,9}, UNSAT@4 -> true count is exactly 3.
def test_start_equals_one_minimum_precondition():
    assert count_multiples_in_range(1, 10, 3) == 3


# --- 5. start == 1 AND end is exactly one less than the next multiple ---
# Boundary: "end = multiple - 1" (first violation point of "end is a multiple").
# CSP: SAT@2 with {3,6}, UNSAT@3 (9 would be next multiple but is excluded).
def test_end_one_less_than_next_multiple_with_start_one():
    assert count_multiples_in_range(1, 8, 3) == 2


# --- 6. divisor == range width (end - start + 1) ---
# Boundary: divisor equals interval width exactly.
# CSP: SAT@1 with {5}, UNSAT@2 (10 excluded since end==9) -> count == 1.
def test_divisor_equals_range_width():
    assert count_multiples_in_range(5, 9, 5) == 1


# --- 7. divisor > range width -> structurally zero multiples ---
# Boundary: divisor exceeds width (13 > 5).
# CSP: UNSAT@1 (no k in [5,9] with k % 13 == 0) -> count == 0.
def test_divisor_larger_than_range_width_gives_zero():
    assert count_multiples_in_range(5, 9, 13) == 0


# --- 8. end is exactly a multiple of divisor ---
# Boundary: "end == multiple" equality point.
# CSP: SAT@3 with {4,8,12}, UNSAT@4 -> count == 3.
def test_end_exactly_a_multiple():
    assert count_multiples_in_range(4, 12, 4) == 3


# --- 9. Minimal valid input allowed by the contract ---
# Boundary: start == end == 1 (smallest possible start), divisor == 1
# (smallest possible divisor) simultaneously.
# CSP: SAT@1, UNSAT@2 (domain has only one possible value) -> count == 1.
def test_minimal_single_element_range_divisor_one():
    assert count_multiples_in_range(1, 1, 1) == 1


# --- 10. Equivalence class (a): normal mid-size range, divisor divides evenly ---
# SMT: proved count == (end-start)//5 + 1 == 9 for (10,50,5)
# (CSP combinatorial check over 9/10 picks in a 41-value domain exceeded the
# solver's 5,000,000-assignment cap, so the arithmetic-identity route was used).
def test_normal_mid_range_multiple_hits():
    assert count_multiples_in_range(10, 50, 5) == 9


# --- 11. Equivalence class (b): divisor much bigger than range -> result 1 ---
# CSP: SAT@1 with {100}, UNSAT@2 (150 excluded) -> count == 1.
def test_large_divisor_yields_one_hit():
    assert count_multiples_in_range(100, 105, 50) == 1


# --- 11b. Equivalence class (b) variant: divisor much bigger than range -> result 0 ---
# CSP: UNSAT@1 (100 excluded since start==101, 150 too big) -> count == 0.
def test_large_divisor_yields_zero_hits():
    assert count_multiples_in_range(101, 105, 50) == 0


# --- 12. Equivalence class (c): start itself is a multiple of divisor ---
# CSP: SAT@4 with {20,24,28,32}, UNSAT@5 -> count == 4.
def test_start_itself_is_multiple():
    assert count_multiples_in_range(20, 35, 4) == 4


# --- 13. Equivalence class (d): start not a multiple, a later value is ---
# CSP: SAT@3 with {24,28,32}, UNSAT@4 -> count == 3.
def test_start_not_multiple_but_later_value_is():
    assert count_multiples_in_range(21, 35, 4) == 3


# --- 14. Out-of-contract robustness probe (NOT required by the documented
# precondition: start < 1 here). Included only to document observed behavior;
# CSP confirms {-3,0,3} are the 3 multiples of 3 in [-5,5] (SAT@3, UNSAT@4),
# and the formula matches even though the precondition is violated, because
# Python's floor division extends the identity to negative start values.
# This is informational, not a contractual requirement.
def test_out_of_contract_negative_start_is_still_consistent():
    assert count_multiples_in_range(-5, 5, 3) == 3


# --- 15. Documented but solver-unverifiable boundary: divisor == 0 ---
# divisor >= 1 is violated at divisor == 0. Z3/SMT-LIB under-specifies
# division by zero, so this boundary cannot be "solver confirmed" the way
# the others are; Python's actual behavior (ZeroDivisionError) is asserted
# directly instead.
def test_divisor_zero_raises():
    with pytest.raises(ZeroDivisionError):
        count_multiples_in_range(1, 10, 0)

import pytest
from target import day_of_year


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Leap-year classification equivalence classes (year % 4 / % 100 / % 400)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def test_leap_div4_not100_2024():
    # Class: year % 4 == 0 and year % 100 != 0 -> LEAP.
    # smt_verify proved And(year%4==0, Or(year%100!=0, year%400==0)) for year=2024.
    # total = prefix(9)=243 + 15 + 1(leap) = 259, proved by smt_verify.
    assert day_of_year(2024, 9, 15) == 259


def test_not_leap_div100_not400_1900():
    # Class: year % 100 == 0 and year % 400 != 0 -> NOT leap (century exception).
    # smt_verify proved Not(leap) for year=1900.
    # total = prefix(9)=243 + 15 + 0 = 258, proved by smt_verify.
    assert day_of_year(1900, 9, 15) == 258


def test_not_leap_div100_not400_2100():
    # Same class as above (century, not div 400), different representative year/month
    # to diversify equivalence-class coverage. smt_verify proved Not(leap) for 2100.
    # total = prefix(6)=151 + 10 + 0 = 161, proved by smt_verify.
    assert day_of_year(2100, 6, 10) == 161


def test_leap_div400_2000():
    # Class: year % 400 == 0 -> LEAP (the exception-to-the-exception).
    # smt_verify proved leap for year=2000.
    # total = prefix(9)=243 + 15 + 1(leap) = 259, proved by smt_verify.
    assert day_of_year(2000, 9, 15) == 259


def test_not_leap_not_div4_2023():
    # Class: year % 4 != 0 -> NOT leap (ordinary case).
    # smt_verify proved Not(leap) for year=2023.
    # total = prefix(9)=243 + 15 + 0 = 258, proved by smt_verify.
    assert day_of_year(2023, 9, 15) == 258


def test_leap_year_but_month_leq_2_no_adjustment():
    # Branch condition "month > 2" is False even though year IS leap (2024).
    # Shows the +1 adjustment never fires for month<=2, regardless of leap-ness.
    # total = prefix(2)=31 + 15 + 0 = 46, proved by smt_verify.
    assert day_of_year(2024, 2, 15) == 46


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. month/day boundary values
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def test_start_of_year():
    # Boundary: month=1, day=1 -> total=1.
    # prefix(1)=0, total=0+1+0=1, proved by smt_verify.
    assert day_of_year(2023, 1, 1) == 1


def test_end_of_non_leap_year():
    # Boundary: month=12, day=31, non-leap year -> total=365.
    # prefix(12)=334, total=334+31+0=365, proved by smt_verify.
    assert day_of_year(2023, 12, 31) == 365


def test_end_of_leap_year():
    # Boundary: month=12, day=31, leap year -> total=366.
    # prefix(12)=334, total=334+31+1=366, proved by smt_verify.
    assert day_of_year(2024, 12, 31) == 366


def test_feb28_leap_year_no_adjustment():
    # Feb boundary (one side of the "month>2" branch guard): month=2 (not >2)
    # so no +1 even in a leap year.
    # prefix(2)=31, total=31+28+0=59, proved by smt_verify.
    assert day_of_year(2024, 2, 28) == 59


def test_feb29_leap_year_no_adjustment():
    # Feb boundary, other side (the leap day itself): still no +1.
    # prefix(2)=31, total=31+29+0=60, proved by smt_verify.
    assert day_of_year(2024, 2, 29) == 60


def test_march1_leap_year_adjustment_kicks_in():
    # Boundary of the "month > 2" branch guard: month becomes 3 (first month
    # where the guard is True) immediately after the Feb 29 leap day.
    # prefix(3)=59, total=59+1+1=61, proved by smt_verify.
    assert day_of_year(2024, 3, 1) == 61


def test_march1_non_leap_year_no_adjustment():
    # Contrast case for the same boundary in a NON-leap year: guard month>2 is
    # True, but leap is False, so no +1.
    # prefix(3)=59, total=59+1+0=60, proved by smt_verify. Together with the
    # previous test this isolates the "+1 only when month>2 AND leap" branch
    # exactly at its activation point.
    assert day_of_year(2023, 3, 1) == 60


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. General equivalence-class representatives (mid-year, month clearly > 2)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def test_mid_year_non_leap():
    # Representative of "ordinary non-leap, month>2" equivalence class.
    # prefix(6)=151, total=151+15+0=166, proved by smt_verify.
    assert day_of_year(2023, 6, 15) == 166


def test_mid_year_leap():
    # Representative of "leap, month>2" equivalence class (same family as
    # test_leap_div4_not100_2024, different month/day).
    # prefix(9)=243, total=243+15+1=259, proved by smt_verify.
    assert day_of_year(2024, 9, 15) == 259


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Counterexamples exposing the missing input-validation abstraction gap
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def test_counterexample_missing_upper_bound_validation():
    # smt_verify counterexample search: assumptions "month>=1, day>=1" (the
    # only checks the function's own code performs -- no upper bounds at all)
    # together with the postcondition "total <= 366" (the true max ordinal in
    # any Gregorian year) is REFUTED. Z3 found year=100, month=7, day=186 ->
    # total=367, i.e. an input that satisfies the (weak) implicit validation
    # but violates the "ordinal is a valid day of the year" postcondition.
    # This demonstrates day_of_year performs NO range validation on month/day.
    assert day_of_year(100, 7, 186) == 367  # exceeds 366, out of any valid range


def test_boundary_month_13_day_1_still_in_range():
    # Boundary for the unvalidated "month" input: month=13 (first violation of
    # the implicit month<=12 constraint) with day=1 lands exactly at 366
    # (proved by smt_verify) -- coincidentally still a "plausible" value,
